items.question: Why did Microsoft's handling of Sydney lead you to write Taming Silicon Valley?
items.object: Taming Silicon Valley and Microsoft's Sydney
items.answer: Well, the reason I wrote the new book is because I sensed a moral decline in Silicon Valley. That's in fact one of the chapter titles is The Moral Decline of Silicon Valley. I particularly sensed it when Microsoft released this product called Sydney and Kevin Roose had this conversation with it in which it told him to get a divorce and all this stuff, and instead of pulling the product, Microsoft just put some Band-Aids on it. And that was a sign to me that things had changed. And within a few days of that, Satya said that we're going to make Google Dance. The whole culture changed, like overnight. And, you know, the antecedent condition, precipitating condition was the popularity of ChatGPT. Suddenly people thought there was real money to be made here and their postures changed entirely. And that worried me because I do think the technology is premature. I do think a lot of harm can come from it, and I kind of dropped what I was doing research wise and really moved full time into policy. And in some ways, the book is actually a memoir. It's not couched that way at all, but it's really a memoir of that time.

The response attributes Silicon Valley's changed posture toward AI to the prospect of profits following ChatGPT's popularity.
The response characterizes Taming Silicon Valley as an implicit memoir of Marcus's move into AI policy.

items.question: How do you assess OpenAI and Anthropic's public support for AI regulation?
items.object: OpenAI and Anthropic's support for regulation
items.answer: Well, I mean, it's hard to get into other people's heads, but I would say that there's more theater than not. You have companies like OpenAI and Anthropic publicly saying they're for AI regulation, and then they're out there trying to weaken whatever regulation is proposed. You know, they all tried to block SB 1047. And ultimately, Anthropic apparently was instrumental in weakening it a good bit at the last minute. You know, OpenAI was—you know, Sam Altman was telling the Senate while I was sitting next to him how important AI regulation is, and behind the scenes, Billy Perrigo reported this in Time magazine, the lobbyists for OpenAI were trying to weaken the UI Act and probably succeeded some. So there's definitely like a two-sidedness to it, where there's public statement that they're supportive and then in private, you know, they really aren't.

items.question: What do you make of GPT-4's ability to play chess?
items.answer: Just as a sidebar on chess. GPT-4 doesn't really play chess that well, so it makes a lot of illegal moves. There's a very good analysis of GPT-4 and chess playing. I'm blanking on the guy's name. And it plays like, I don't know, like a 1600 game, which is better than the average person in your high school, but not anything like world class. And it makes a lot of illegal moves, like 6% of the time or something, some crazy number like that, which, no, you know, compare with a chess computer that I bought in 1979 where you could stick the little pieces in the hole. I think it was called Sargon, was the software underlying that. It never made an illegal move. Never, ever. Right. We're talking about chess software from—I mean, really even further back, 1969—never made illegal moves like GPT-4 is not state of the art in chess. And we should understand that. But people don't. They're amazed that it can do it at all. And there's some reason why you should be amazed that it can do it at all. But you have to realize that it is not, you know, searching a tree the way that a proper chess program can do it. It's doing mimicry.

items.question: How would you explain a language model producing better chess moves when its opponent plays more sophisticated chess?
items.answer: Well, it is a mimic. You're directing the system to a particular part of its corpus, so you can direct it towards the more sophisticated language or the less sophisticated language or whatever, and it's going to try to replicate language like that. And so that is why you get some of those kinds of effects. I don't know whether what Carlini described really bears out in a systematic study, but if it did, that would be my guess for why it would, is like the database of lousy chess games is going to look different from the database of good chess games.
quotes: Well, it is a mimic.

You're directing the system to a particular part of its corpus, so you can direct it towards the more sophisticated language or the less sophisticated language or whatever, and it's going to try to replicate language like that. And so that is why you get some of those kinds of effects. items.question: What lesson do you draw from cigarette manufacturers' historical demands for stronger scientific evidence of harm?
items.object: Cigarette manufacturers' demands for causal evidence
items.answer: So just to make clear, the cigarette manufacturers pretended for years that there was no conceivable harm. They said the science here isn't good enough. Let's wait until—I mean, basically, the cigarette manufacturers wanted to say, unless you do a causal study in which you assign human beings to smoking cigarettes or not, this is not science, and we're not responsible. And they got away with that for a really long time. Now, if you're an actual scientist, you understand that you can use animal models and you can do certain kinds of observational things, and you make a pretty darn good guess that cigarettes cause lung cancer without actually doing the experiment that they were insisting on. But they just, you know, with a straight face would say this stuff for years. And a lot of people died.

The response states that evidence from animal models and observational research can support the conclusion that cigarettes cause lung cancer without randomized human smoking experiments.

items.question: Where do you draw the line between allowing AI research and allowing commercial AI deployment?
items.answer: Yeah. I mean, I think a lot of the stuff that we have now should actually be in the lab and not commercially deployed at large scale. So I have no problem with people researching AI, trying to find—I mean, all my issues are around deployment. So for example, we know that gen AI is being used to make health care decisions and job decisions and so forth. And we know that there is likely to be discrimination there, but we don't have public access to how bad the problem even is, how much bias there is. But there are almost certainly bias against minority groups, for example, in using LLMs to make job decisions. And this is just not good. And I'm sure it's happening literally every day, at large scale now.

items.question: Why do you think existing defamation law may be inadequate for large language models?
items.answer: Here's another one where it's still very ambiguous, which is defamation. Large language models have, for example, accused people of sexual harassment that they did not actually commit. We know that they didn't commit it. But it's not clear that the people who were defamed by this have any recourse whatsoever, because the existing laws of defamation—there's a bunch of complications here. It hasn't really been cashed out in court how it's all going to go. But typically there's some notion of intending malice. Well, you could argue that large language models don't have emotions. They don't have malice. They're not doing it on purpose. It's actually a kind of negligence that's making them do this. But are we going to say that you can make a system that's arbitrarily negligent to the point of really screwing up people's lives, perhaps, just because they work differently from people? That doesn't seem to make sense to me. I would say the existing laws don't clearly handle what happens if some AI system completely negligently defames a person and is completely negligent because there is no fact-checking on top of these systems. So my favorite example of hallucination is not particularly defamatory. One of these systems said I had a pet chicken named Henrietta. I don't think that really causes me any harm in the world, but there's also nothing I can do to stop it. And there are other cases like, you know, a certain law school professor was accused of sexual harassment, and there's probably nothing he can do about it.

items.question: Why would you oppose using current AI-text detectors to identify student papers written by language models?
items.answer: So, like, if you're talking about, for example, could we use these pieces of software that look for LLMs to, I don't know, weed out student papers, let's say 75%, 70% correct or 80% correct or whatever, is just not good enough. I mean, imagine you're the student who wrote the good paper that is described as an LLM. You're going to be really, really upset if you're in that one in five who got screwed, and justly so. And so you can't, or you shouldn't, be using software that's that bad at a task like that. And you really have to be better. Nobody knows how to make a 99% accurate LM detector.

items.question: Why do you consider AI alignment important despite disagreeing with strong extinction narratives?
items.answer: Well, I mean, I think that goes to the part that I think really is important, even though I disagree about the strong extinction narratives. The part that I think is important is we need two things. We need a global agreement about how we're going to handle AI as it gets more dangerous, sharing information and things like that. And we need technical means for alignment. And that will only get more important as AI is empowered more, which is to say, given more responsibility in the world and as it actually gets more proficient in doing the things that it is asked to do, because there will be more opportunities for bad actors to do bad things. And you want your system to actually be able to calculate, is this going to have an adverse effect on a large part of humanity? Then I shouldn't follow this instruction. You actually—I mean, the risks aren't wrong to want something like that.

items.question: How do you distinguish your skepticism about current AI from your views on possible future AGI?
items.answer: I mean, it's one thing for a system to have a model of where objects are and so forth, but there's a certain level of agency and consciousness that a bunch of people, including at this conference that we were just at, would like to see happen. And I do not want to see happen. I think it just opens another barrel of worms. It's not like I think that's imminent. And you have to understand that most of my skepticism about AI is skepticism about what we can do right now and overclaiming about current capabilities. I think AGI is possible. I don't expect to see it next week. And I offered Elon Musk a $1 million bet when he said that he thought it would happen by 2025, and I would still love if he would make that bet, because it's easy money. And why not? Even if it goes to charity, I'd be happy to make the bet. Elon is still there, and I have a friend who will raise it to 10 million if you're in. I don't think AGI is close, but I don't see any principled reason why it's impossible. I've never seen a good argument for that.

items.question: What most troubles you about Chinese AI regulation?
items.answer: Well, I mean, the thing that I object to most in Chinese AI regulation, which is actually much stronger than US AI regulation, is an insistence that everything be consistent with the party line. And I would not like to see that in the United States. I don't like seeing it in China. It's not as much my business, or maybe none of my business, if they do that in China. I certainly don't want anything like that in the United States, ever. You know, it's not legal to operate a chatbot if it doesn't conform to what the state believes. So it's one thing to say chatbots shouldn't promote conspiracy theories that are clearly false or whatever. I can imagine something in that direction, but becoming an instrument of the ruling party? No. I don't think anybody on the planet should do it. I can't stop China from doing it. But I think it's wrong that China is doing it.

items.question: Why do you worry that OpenAI could become a major surveillance company?
items.answer:
So already you had this situation where they're clearly trying to get everything they possibly can about you and to commercialize it, probably to sell ads. And then they bought a webcam company. I was just like, what? Like they're having a lot of trouble actually making money at OpenAI. They lost, you know, operating loss, costs relative to revenue last year, $5 billion. A lot of companies tried their software and are not that excited about it, having tried it out. Copilot, which is run on their platform. A lot of people aren't that happy with it. Microsoft is trying to rush people to use the product. Everybody tried it. It's not like there was a lack of marketing, but it's not that reliable. So OpenAI is faced with a problem. How are we going to make money off of this stuff? And it's not cheap, right? I mean, they've probably spent whatever $10 billion on data and chips, and they're going to spend another ten or whatever. And GPT-4, who knows how expensive. They need to make money, or they will either go out of business or Microsoft will take a bigger chunk of them. It's not clear that VCs are going to want to up their valuation to $200 billion, given the kind of picture of revenue that is emerging.

And so if I were Sam Altman and I had a different kind of morality than I think I do, the first thing I would think about is surveillance, right? People are giving them all this data on a silver platter. Now you got a camera, too. That's the natural direction for the company to go. Despite their name, OpenAI. It's a really sinister thing for them to do, to become Big Brother. And did I mention they're still a nonprofit? Which is insane. So we may very well wind up with the world's largest surveillance company as a wholly owned subsidiary of a place that calls themselves OpenAI, that's nonprofit. That is, I think, almost a default outcome right now. And that's, to me, upsetting.

items.question: Why are you skeptical that language-model characters will sustain an engaging metaverse?
items.answer: I think a lot of people imagine you could populate a metaverse world with large language model characters, and I think that that's going to get tired fast because those characters aren't really going to understand the world. And so it'll work for a little while, having non-player characters made by chatbots. But eventually things are not going to make sense and it's going to break the illusion. The only way metaverse is going to work is if the illusion is so potent and it's so much fun to play with. And the more that you have these weird experiences. Like today I had Grok. I asked it to make 11 eggs without an egg carton, and instead it made 15 with an egg carton.

items.question: Why do you think recent language-model results undermine the claim that scaling is producing exponential progress?
items.object: Scaling language models and the NYT Connections benchmark
items.answer:
Looking at PaLM, Chinchilla, which was state of the art in April 2022, and relative to release dates when GPT-4 came out, you could genuinely make the argument that we saw exponential progress over that period. It was pretty amazing what happened. There was a lot of progress, and you could argue GPT-4 was kind of an outlier. But is it continuing? Each data point is a test of the hypothesis that scaling would continue at the pace it did from PaLM/Chinchilla to GPT-4. It's obvious that scaling has slowed; we're not still on that exponential regime.

There are multiple possible explanations. One is we don't have enough compute. Maybe true, maybe not. A lot of companies are spending a lot of money. I'm not sure compute is actually the bottleneck. Another one is data. It was a neat trick to take a tenth or hundredth of the internet and then switch to having more or less all the internet, but you can't now throw 100 times the internet because that doesn't exist. I think there's an architectural problem: these things don't have representations of the world, and so there are always outlier cases.

We have what psychologists call a ceiling effect, so it's not reasonable to expect 100% per se. The point still holds. I did another test: I looked at NYT Connections, the little game my family loves to play in The New York Times, where you have to find clusters of categories. We're nowhere near ceiling on that, and we're still finding—I did this in April—we found GPT-4 Turbo was barely better than GPT-4. We don't have as thorough data for Connections as we do for MMLU, but I think the point is clear.

items.question: What do you see as the lasting significance of your 1998 work on neural-network generalization?
items.answer:
One reason, going back to work I did in 1998 when I was a kid, is that they don't generalize well. They generalize a little bit, and that makes it incredibly confusing for people who haven't thought about this carefully. People say, “Neural networks generalize, and we need generalization, so we're good.” But we need two kinds of generalization: to things nearby the things we trained on, and a broader form of generalization. What I showed in 1998, and what I think is still my most important work, was that multilayer perceptrons, the forerunner to today's systems, if trained on something as simple as the identity function for even binary numbers, would generalize to other even binary numbers they hadn't seen before. I called that within-training-space generalization. But they wouldn't generalize beyond it to bigger numbers or odd numbers. I showed this was true of a whole bunch of models and talked about why it followed from backpropagation.

For a long time nobody listened at all. I was accused of having a terrorist attack on AI in one peer review for the article in which I ultimately published this. Now I think everybody realizes this is a problem. We call it distribution shift or something like that. That is the fundamental problem—not the only problem, but the fundamental problem. If you move away from the distribution, these systems just aren't very good. I made that argument in 2021 when I was here, and I've been making it for 30 years. I'm getting tired of it, but it's still true. We are not going to get to AGI if we don't solve that problem.

items.question: Why do you favor hybrid systems as a foundation for robust artificial intelligence?
items.answer:
One thing I argued for then and the last time I gave a keynote at this conference three years ago was that we need a hybrid approach. It seems obvious to me now; it seemed obvious then. We can't get to AI by doing deep learning alone. Deep learning alone is good for some kinds of learning, but it's poor for abstraction. It's still poor for abstraction. How can you not understand the concept of current prime minister of Italy, having been trained on the entire internet? Something is wrong there. Classical AI obviously isn't very good at learning from large amounts of data. We have to build hybrid systems.

Part of the point I made in the 2020 article and when I was here is that even having neurosymbolic AI, a hybrid approach, is not a panacea. It's not the end of the story. People are looking for one magic bullet, the one algorithm to rule them all, and they love LLMs as a candidate for that. We're never going to find that. We're also going to need large-scale knowledge, like Doug Lenat liked to think about. We need ways to represent knowledge about space, time, and causality, like what is now. Hybrid models that build in some knowledge in a special domain still do much better. I gave the example then of AlphaFold, and now I would give AlphaGeometry, which builds in some knowledge and is a hybrid system and does better.

We need reasoning. We need cognitive models—what is a cognitive model? Yann LeCun likes to call them world models, which is also a perfectly fine term. That's a model of the world where you have entities and know the relationships between them. You should have that in a transparent way, so you can look up in some database who is the current prime minister of Italy, then draw a picture of the person.

items.question: How do you assess the progress represented by current driverless-car services?
items.answer:
Driverless cars have made progress since 2021. Some of that progress has been winnowing out the also-rans, so we have fewer companies. They're actually in demos now, but they are still demos. I was excited to read yesterday that Waymo is finally going to try to deal with snow. That's cool that they're finally trying to deal with snow. Roughly speaking, we have about 15 cities where you can take a genuinely driverless car. What we learned from Cruise is that genuinely driverless cars that have no driver in the car still have remote operations. Cruise had more people in the remote operations than they had cars on the road. Waymo hasn't published that number, but at least those are genuinely driverless cars in the sense there is no driver in the car.

You can only use them in about 10 cities, and no rural areas that I know about. I looked up how many cities there are in the world, not using a chatbot, and got the answer of 10,000. Your chance of being able to use a driverless car if you don't live in the Bay Area or in Arizona is very low. It's still a demo. We still don't have them on the road. You still need to pay attention if you're in a Tesla, etc.

items.question: How do you explain venture capitalists funding AI bets that you regard as economically doubtful?
items.answer:
How does the venture capital industry work? Why are people making what look like actually bad bets if you take a step back? It's because they make most of their money right now on fees rather than what they call the carry. The fee is they get 2%; it's called two and 20, so they get 20% of any big profit and they get 2% of the money they're administering. If a venture capitalist can find a bet that sounds plausible to other people, they can make 2% on the bet. If it's a big bet, that's 2% on a lot of money. You get some pension fund to make a billion-dollar bet and you get 2% of that; that's a pretty nice year right there. You're done.

There's every incentive in the world for these VCs to find things that sound plausible, and the hype helps make it sound plausible. Some VCs are really good and in it for the long game, but a lot aren't. They'll go with the hypey thing, and if it's one they can justify as a billion-dollar bet or a $20 billion bet, they love that. Why are the pension funds doing this? Because the pension fund managers work on the same thing. They'll be gone by the time this all collapses.

items.question: Why do you find OpenAI's description of its training data as publicly available and private sources inadequate?
items.answer:
One important thing is we need transparency. We need a full accounting, for example, of what data is used to train the current generation of models. We don't have that; we don't know. We have a company called OpenAI that will not tell you what data they're using. Mira Murati went on television, a Wall Street Journal interview, I guess, and said, “We use publicly available and private sources.” That's all she was willing to say, and that's what they say in their papers.

“Publicly available” is a weasel word. Some of it is stuff they licensed, some is public domain for the taking, and some of it is not, but they were able to get it from some copy on Reddit, so they downloaded it. It's a real weasel word, and it doesn't tell you any specifics. It matters because we can't fix it if we don't know what data goes in. These systems are so dependent on the data. It matters because we don't know what bias is there; we can't in general mitigate the risk.

items.question: Why might useful applications of language models fail to prevent another AI winter?
items.object: Useful AI applications and the prospect of an AI winter
items.answer:
I understand the perspective, and you could be right. I can't predict with perfect certainty, and some of it is an economic question. There are applications of LLMs, as you say. The LLMs can be integrated and so forth. Some of it's a question of economics: how much money is there in these applications that are not the thing everyone was promised, and how is all this going to shake out? If the narrower applications you're describing make a few billion dollars a year, but people have been investing imagining trillions of dollars in payoff, it's a question of how people feel about that. Some of it's a vibe.

There's definitely some real-world applications; some are important. If there's one really good biotech application, maybe that justifies the whole thing and forestalls the winter, or maybe it doesn't. It's about how the vibes go and the economics, the cost of the chips versus the benefits.

It could be that we have a winter when we shouldn't. There could be a couple of really nice medical applications that don't make that much money but really save a lot of lives, perhaps for rare diseases, helping people who couldn't otherwise be helped. I'm making up the example, but you can imagine things like that where we should actually keep doing this, but people say, “Yeah, but the chips are too expensive, and I don't want to do it anymore.” I don't know. It's an interesting and open question where it will go. I think we actually agree on the parameters: there is a bubble around generative AI, it is going to have an impact, and there are some practical real-world applications. We're both trying to guess the balance of that, and neither of us really know. It's hard to know.
